title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was introduced. The expanded summary of the House passed version is repeated here.)

Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016

(Sec. 5) This bill allows civil claims or causes of action for the recovery of artwork or certain other property lost between January 1, 1933, and December 31, 1945, because of Nazi persecution to be commenced within six years after the claimant's actual discovery of: (1) the identity and location of the artwork or other property, and (2) a possessory interest in the artwork or property.

Such statutory limitation period of six years after actual discovery preempts any other statutes of limitation or defenses relating to the passage of time.

Preexisting claims known by a claimant before enactment of this bill shall be considered discovered on the date of this bill's enactment if they were barred before, or not barred on, the date of enactment.

This bill applies to claims or actions that are: (1) pending on the date of this bill's enactment, including an action for which the time to file an appeal has not expired; or (2) filed after enactment but before 2027. But the bill does not apply to claims barred on the day before enactment of this bill if: (1) the claimant had knowledge on or after January 1, 1999, and (2) six years have passed from the date such claimant acquired such knowledge and during which time the claim was not barred by a statute of limitations.

summary.headline: This law gives people more time to sue to recover art and property taken by Nazis between 1933 and 1945, measured from when they discover the item and their claim to it.
summary.what_it_does: The law sets a six-year deadline for filing a civil lawsuit to recover artwork or other property lost because of Nazi persecution between January 1, 1933, and December 31, 1945. The six years start when the owner actually discovers where the item is and has a claim to it. This deadline overrides other time limits or defenses based on how much time has passed. The law also covers older claims that were already known before it was enacted, and it applies to cases pending on the enactment date or filed before 2027, with an exception for certain claims that had already expired.

who_it_affects.group: Heirs and original owners of artwork or property seized during Nazi persecution
who_it_affects.how: They get a longer window, measured from discovery, to file lawsuits seeking the return of their property.

who_it_affects.group: Museums, galleries, and private holders of possibly looted art
who_it_affects.how: They may face lawsuits over works with Nazi-era ownership gaps that might previously have been protected by old filing deadlines.
They must apply the six-year discovery-based deadline in place of other time limits for qualifying cases.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 16, 2016; the law applies to qualifying claims pending on that date or filed before 2027.
